financials.key_finding:
Advanced Micro Devices has undergone a decade-long financial metamorphosis that culminated in record results across every material metric in 2025. Full-year 2025 revenue reached $34.6 billion, up 34 percent from $25.8 billion in FY2024, with non-GAAP operating income of $7.8 billion — a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 22.5 percent — and non-GAAP net income of $6.8 billion, or $4.17 per diluted share, each records for the company. GAAP results were weaker due to amortisation of the Xilinx and Pensando acquisition intangibles: GAAP gross margin was 50 percent versus 52 percent non-GAAP, and GAAP operating income was $3.7 billion versus the $7.8 billion non-GAAP figure, reflecting approximately $4 billion in acquisition-related intangible amortisation and stock-based compensation charges embedded in the GAAP structure.

The Q1 2026 earnings report, released May 5, 2026, reinforced the growth trajectory: revenue of $10.253 billion was up 38 percent year-over-year, non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 55 percent, non-GAAP operating income reached $2.540 billion, and non-GAAP diluted EPS was $1.37, up 43 percent year-over-year. The company guided Q2 2026 revenue of approximately $11.2 billion with non-GAAP gross margin of approximately 56 percent — a sequential expansion that management attributed to favourable Data Center product mix as higher-ASP Instinct and EPYC units take a larger share of the revenue base. If AMD executes to the Q2 guidance midpoint, the annualised first-half 2026 run rate would imply full-year revenue approaching $45 billion even before the typically stronger second half.

Analyst consensus as of May 2026 projects full-year 2026 revenue of approximately $48.4 billion and non-GAAP EPS of approximately $4.99. Against a stock price of approximately $512 and a market capitalisation of approximately $821 billion, AMD trades at roughly 58 times consensus 2026 non-GAAP earnings and an EV/EBITDA of approximately 88 times on a last-twelve-months basis — 97 percent above AMD's own ten-year median EV/EBITDA of 44.7 times. Capital structure is conservative: long-term debt is approximately $1.7 billion against cash and equivalents of approximately $5.1 billion as of Q1 2026, implying a net cash position and ample capacity for continued share repurchases and R&D investment. Free cash flow generation was described by CFO Jean Hu as 'record quarterly free cash flow' in Q1 2026, indicating the asset-light fabless model is translating increasing revenue at high incremental margins.
structural_observations: Revenue base and segmentation: AMD's $34.6 billion FY2025 revenue comprises four segments — Data Center ($16.6B, 48% of total), Client and Gaming ($14.6B, 42%), Embedded ($3.5B, 10%) — with Data Center now the primary earnings engine. Data Center grew 32% in FY2025 and 57% in Q1 2026; at the Q1 2026 run rate of $5.775B per quarter, the annualised Data Center revenue exceeds $23 billion, approaching the company's entire FY2022 revenue of $23.6 billion.

Fiscal year cadence: AMD operates a 52/53-week fiscal year ending on the last Saturday of December, giving FY2025 a year-end of December 27, 2025 and FY2024 a year-end of December 28, 2024. This creates occasional 53-week fiscal years that investors should adjust for in year-over-year comparisons.

Margin progression: GAAP gross margin expanded from approximately 46% in FY2023 to 50% in FY2025; non-GAAP gross margin expanded from approximately 51% to 52% over the same period, with Q4 2025 non-GAAP gross margin reaching 57% and Q1 2026 reaching 55%. Management guidance implies 56% for Q2 2026 and steady expansion toward 58–60% over the 2026–2028 horizon as Data Center, which carries the highest segment-level margins, grows its revenue share. The GAAP/non-GAAP gap of approximately 200–500 basis points reflects amortisation of the roughly $26 billion in Xilinx and Pensando acquisition intangibles over useful lives of 5–15 years.

Capital structure: AMD maintains a conservative balance sheet with approximately $1.7 billion in long-term debt (7.50% Senior Notes due 2022 and 2.95% Senior Notes due 2024 have been retired; remaining maturities are laddered through 2052) and approximately $5.1 billion in cash and short-term investments as of Q1 2026. The net cash position and robust free cash flow generation support an active share repurchase programme — the board has authorised $6 billion in buybacks as of 2024 — without constraining R&D investment, which has run at approximately $5–6 billion annually.

Debt versus equity financing: AMD is equity-financed for its growth phase. The Xilinx acquisition was an all-stock transaction valued at $49 billion at announcement (October 2020) and approximately $35 billion at close (February 2022). The dilution from that issuance has been partially offset by subsequent buybacks, and the share count has stabilised near 1.65 billion diluted shares. AMD does not pay a dividend; all capital is returned via repurchases or reinvested in R&D and capex.

Comparable peer group: AMD's direct financial comparables are NVIDIA Corporation (semiconductor AI infrastructure), Intel Corporation (x86 CPU), and, for the Embedded segment, Lattice Semiconductor and Microchip Technology. On AI GPU revenue AMD is the number-two player; NVIDIA's Data Center revenue reached $194 billion in its FY2026 (year ended January 2026), making NVIDIA approximately 11 times the scale of AMD's Data Center segment. Intel's data centre business has been declining and restructuring under CEO Lip-Bu Tan.

Market capitalisation volatility: AMD's market cap has swung dramatically: from approximately $3 billion when Lisa Su became CEO in 2014, to $200 billion at peak AI enthusiasm in late 2021, down to approximately $80 billion during the 2022 semiconductor correction, recovering to approximately $300 billion in 2023 as MI300X demand exceeded expectations, and reaching approximately $821 billion by May 2026 after the Q1 2026 earnings beat. This volatility reflects AMD's sensitivity to AI capital expenditure cycles, PC market conditions, and sentiment around its ability to challenge NVIDIA's software moat.

leadership.key_finding:
Advanced Micro Devices is operationally and strategically dominated by Dr. Lisa Su, who has served as president, CEO, and since 2022, board chair. Her tenure since October 2014 represents one of the most celebrated corporate turnarounds in semiconductor history: she led the internal development of the Zen CPU microarchitecture, renegotiated AMD's manufacturing relationship with TSMC to access leading-edge nodes, oversaw the $49 billion all-stock acquisition of Xilinx in 2022, and has directed AMD's aggressive positioning in AI accelerators through the Instinct product line. Su was born in Taiwan and immigrated to the United States as a child; she earned three degrees from MIT in electrical engineering and worked at Texas Instruments, IBM (rising to VP of the Semiconductor R&D Center), and Freescale Semiconductor before joining AMD in 2012. She has been named to Fortune's Most Powerful Women list numerous times and received the IEEE Robert Noyce Medal in 2024. Her total compensation package for FY2025 was not yet publicly disclosed at the frozen snapshot date but was approximately $30–40 million in prior years, comprising base salary, cash bonus tied to revenue and earnings targets, and equity awards with multi-year vesting.

Financial leadership transitioned to Jean Hu, who joined AMD as executive vice president, CFO, and treasurer from Marvell Technology, where she had served as CFO since 2016. Hu has overseen AMD's transition to a $30+ billion revenue business and has communicated a clear capital allocation philosophy prioritising R&D investment, targeted M&A, and share buybacks over dividends. The board of directors, chaired by Su, includes KC McClure (appointed January 2025, former Accenture CFO), John Caldwell (Lead Independent Director, semiconductor industry veteran), Nora Denzel, Mark Durcan (former Micron Technology CEO), Michael Inglis (ARM Holdings background), Joseph Papermaster (AMD CTO, non-voting advisory capacity in board processes), and Abhi Talwalkar (former LSI Corporation CEO). AMD has no controlling private equity or strategic shareholder; the largest institutional holders are Vanguard Group (approximately 8–9%), BlackRock (approximately 7–8%), and State Street (approximately 4–5%).
research_notes_for_writer: Lisa Su compensation structure: The chapter writer should pull AMD's most recent DEF 14A (proxy statement) filed with SEC EDGAR to obtain the precise Summary Compensation Table for Su, Hu, and other named executive officers. The proxy will include base salary, annual bonus payout vs. target, equity grant details, and the performance metrics used. AMD's proxy is typically filed in March/April following fiscal year-end.

Su's relationship with TSMC: Investigate the depth and exclusivity of AMD's TSMC partnership, including whether AMD has signed long-term capacity reservation agreements (LTAs) similar to Apple's, and whether AMD has paid any prepayments or reservation fees for 2nm capacity for the Venice CPU and MI400 GPU. TSMC's annual report and AMD's 10-K risk factors are primary sources.

Board independence and potential conflicts: John Caldwell's history as interim CEO of AMD from 2011–2012 and his role as lead independent director while Su is both CEO and chair is worth examining for governance implications. The 2022 and 2023 proxy statements discuss the board's rationale for combined CEO/Chair role.

Jean Hu's specific financial decisions: The chapter writer should examine Hu's public commentary on capital allocation — specifically AMD's approach to R&D intensity (as percentage of revenue), the pace and terms of share repurchases, and any forward guidance on operating leverage targets as the business scales toward $50B revenue. Earnings call transcripts on AMD's IR site and SEC 8-K filings contain verbatim CFO remarks.

Xilinx leadership integration: The former Xilinx CEO Victor Peng joined AMD as president following the 2022 acquisition close and departed in 2023. The chapter writer should investigate whether Xilinx's original management team is retained and how AMD has integrated FPGA product leadership — the Embedded segment's recovery or further decline partly depends on this.

Succession planning: AMD's proxy disclosures on executive succession and board refreshment are worth examining, especially given Su's stature — her departure would represent a material risk that markets likely do not fully price. The board's nominating and governance committee disclosures describe the framework.

Stock ownership: Su's direct stock ownership and any planned sales under 10b5-1 plans are disclosed in Form 4 filings on EDGAR. The writer should review recent Form 4s to contextualise whether insiders are net buyers or sellers at current price levels near $512.
